General.Description:
Viktor Sorokin was a senior cultural attaché at the Soviet Embassy in Vienna when he decided to defect. He was forty-one years old, had a wife and two children in Moscow, and had spent twenty years building a career within a system he had come to understand — with the slow, reluctant certainty of someone who cannot any longer pretend not to see — was built on a lie.

The decision took a decade to make. The act itself took forty minutes. What followed — the safe house, the debriefing rooms, the long silence about whether his family had been punished for his choice, the process of becoming a man with a new name in a country that was not his own — took the rest of his life.

The Long Road is an autobiography of extraordinary restraint and extraordinary emotional depth. Sorokin is not interested in the thriller narrative of espionage memoirs. He is interested in the interior life of a man who chose freedom and lived with the permanent knowledge of what that choice cost.

Published originally in German in 1994, this new English translation by Natasha Bremer restores passages cut from earlier editions and includes a new afterword by Sorokin written six months before his death in 2021.

A testament to the complicated meaning of liberty.
